chapters.name: Chapter 1: Safe, strong mentoring with AI

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The mentor's role and safety rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the safety rules you will follow every time you meet a young person.
This lesson builds toward: Every time you meet a young person, you will follow your program's safety rules and the steps to take if a young person tells you about harm, naming at least five rules and the reporting steps without help.
A mentor is a trusted adult who listens, encourages and helps a young person set and reach goals. You are not their parent, teacher or therapist; you are a steady, caring guide.
Programs protect young people and mentors with rules. Common ones: a background check before you start, meeting in public or approved places, a second adult nearby instead of being alone with a young person, contact only through approved channels, and never giving rides, gifts or money unless your program allows it. Your program's policy is the rule to follow.
If a young person tells you they are being hurt or are in danger, stay calm, listen, do not promise to keep it secret, and follow your program's reporting steps right away. In an emergency call 911. The Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline is (800) 422-4453.
Step by step:
- Complete your program's background check and training.
- Meet only in public or approved places, with another adult nearby.
- Use only approved ways to contact your mentee.
- If a young person tells you about harm: listen, do not promise secrecy, follow reporting steps.
Words to know:
- Mentor: a trusted adult who guides and encourages a young person.
- Mentee: the young person being mentored.
- Background check: a check of a person's records before they work with young people.
Official sources:
- Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline
- MENTOR: Elements of Effective Practice for Mentoring
Try it now: Find your program's mentoring policy (or ask the coordinator). Write down five rules you will follow every time you meet your mentee.
You can now explain a mentor's role and the safety rules you follow.

options: A steady, caring guide who listens and encourages
check.why: A mentor is a trusted adult guide, not a parent, teacher or therapist.

check.q: Your mentee asks for a ride home after a session. What do you do?
options: Give the ride; it is kind
Follow your program's policy on rides
Ask them to keep it secret
Let them walk alone at night
check.why: Never give rides unless your program allows it; the policy is the rule.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Planning a session with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a free AI assistant to plan a 45-minute session with a clear goal.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will plan a 45-minute session with a warm-up, an activity, a talk and next steps, giving AI only general details and checking the plan for safety, cost and fit.
A good session has four parts: a warm-up (5 minutes), an activity (20 minutes), a talk about what you learned (15 minutes) and a plan for next time (5 minutes).
A free AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini can suggest activities. Describe the young person in general terms only: age group, interests and goal. Example: "Plan a 45-minute mentoring session for a 14-year-old who loves basketball and wants to raise a math grade. Include a warm-up, a low-cost activity and three questions."
Never give AI a young person's name, school, address, photos, family problems or anything they told you in trust. Then check the plan: Is it safe, free or cheap, and right for this young person?
Step by step:
- Pick one goal for the session.
- Describe the mentee in general terms only: age, interests, goal.
- Ask AI for a warm-up, activity and questions.
- Check the plan for safety, cost and fit, and change what does not fit.
Words to know:
- Session: one meeting between a mentor and mentee.
- Warm-up: a short, easy start that helps people relax.
Try it now: Ask AI to plan a 45-minute session for a young person you mentor or might mentor, using only general details. Change one part so it fits better.
You can now plan a mentoring session with AI while protecting the young person's privacy.

check.q: How long is the activity in the 45-minute session plan?
check.why: The plan is a 5-minute warm-up, 20-minute activity, 15-minute talk and 5-minute next steps.

check.q: AI suggests a paid trip to a theme park for your session. What do you do?
options: Ask the mentee's family to pay
Change it to a free or low-cost activity that fits
check.why: You check AI's plan for safety, cost and fit, and change what does not fit.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Asking good questions and really listening
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write three open questions and practice listening without fixing.
This lesson builds toward: In a conversation with a young person, you will ask open questions and repeat back what you heard before giving advice, using at least three open questions in your own words.
Closed questions get one-word answers: "Was school good?" "Yes." Open questions invite a real answer: "What was the best part of your week?" "What is something you want to get better at?"
Listening matters more than talking. Look at them, put your phone away, nod, and repeat back what you heard: "So the math test felt unfair because you studied the wrong chapter?" Do not rush to fix everything; ask what they think they could try.
AI can suggest conversation starters for different moods and interests. Ask it for ten open questions for a teen who loves music, then pick the three that sound most like you.
Step by step:
- Turn closed questions into open ones.
- Put your phone away and give full attention.
- Repeat back what you heard.
- Ask what they think they could try before giving advice.
Words to know:
- Open question: a question that cannot be answered with yes or no.
- Active listening: listening closely and repeating back what you heard.
Try it now: Ask AI for ten open questions for a young person with a hobby you know about. Pick three, and rewrite them in your own words.
You can now ask open questions and listen in a way that helps young people talk.

options: One that invites a real answer, not just yes or no
A question with only one right answer
A question asked in a loud voice
check.why: Open questions invite young people to share more than one word.

check.q: Your mentee says practice was terrible. What do you say first?
options: "So practice felt really hard today. What happened?"
check.why: Repeating back what you heard and asking more shows you are listening.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Helping young people use AI well

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Honest AI use for school
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Show a young person how to use AI as a tutor, not to do their work.
This lesson builds toward: When a young person uses AI for school, you will demonstrate honest AI use to explain, quiz and give feedback, and check its answers, following the school's and the tool's rules and never turning in AI's work.
Many students already use AI. Schools have different rules: some allow it for some tasks, some do not. Always check the school's and teacher's rules first. Many AI tools also have minimum age rules and may need a parent's or guardian's permission for teens; check each tool's terms with the parent or guardian.
Honest use means AI helps you learn, not that it does the work for you. Good uses: "Explain fractions like I'm 12." "Quiz me on these vocabulary words." "Give me feedback on my paragraph, but do not rewrite it." Copying AI's answers and turning them in as your own is cheating.
Teach them to check AI too. It can be wrong. Compare with the textbook, class notes or the teacher.
Step by step:
- Check the school's and teacher's AI rules.
- Check the tool's age rules with a parent or guardian.
- Use AI to explain, quiz or give feedback.
- Never turn in AI's work as your own.
- Check answers against class materials.
Words to know:
- Tutor: someone or something that helps you learn, not does the work for you.
- Cheating: turning in work that is not your own as if it were.
Try it now: With your mentee (or on your own to practice), ask AI to explain one topic from school in simple words and then quiz you with three questions. Check one answer against a textbook or class notes.
You can now show a young person how to use AI honestly as a study helper.

check.q: Which is a good AI request for school?
options: "Give me feedback on my paragraph, but do not rewrite it."
check.why: Asking for feedback helps the student learn while doing their own work.

check.q: Your 12-year-old mentee wants to sign up for an AI tool. What do you do first?
options: Sign them up with your email
Tell them to lie about their age
Check the tool's age rules with a parent or guardian
check.why: Many AI tools have age rules that need a parent's or guardian's check.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Exploring careers and goals together
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI and an official site to explore one career with your mentee.
This lesson builds toward: Given a young person's interests, you will explore careers with AI and check one on bls.gov/ooh, ending with one small next step and a date.
Young people often know only the jobs they see around them. Exploring careers opens doors. Start with what they love: games, music, sports, fixing things, helping people, drawing.
Ask AI: "List five careers for a teen who loves video games and art. For each, say what the job is in one sentence and what to study." Then look up one job together on the Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov/ooh, the free U.S. government guide, to check its pay, training and job outlook.
Turn interest into a small goal: join a club, take a free class at the library, talk to someone who does that job, or try a free online lesson.
Step by step:
- Ask about what they love.
- Ask AI for five related careers.
- Look up one on bls.gov/ooh together.
- Set one small next step with a date.
Words to know:
- Career: the kind of work someone does over many years.
- Job outlook: how fast a job is expected to grow.
Official sources:
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Occupational Outlook Handbook
Try it now: Pick an interest (yours or your mentee's). Ask AI for five related careers, check one on bls.gov/ooh, and write one small next step with a date.
You can now help a young person explore careers and set a small, real next step.

check.q: What does the Occupational Outlook Handbook show for a job?
check.why: The Handbook at bls.gov/ooh shows a job's pay, training and outlook.

check.q: Your mentee likes drawing and the AI lists graphic designer. What is a good next step?
options: Tell them it is not a real job
Set one small step, like a free class at the library, with a date
Pick a different career for them
check.why: Turning interest into a small dated step builds momentum.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Tracking progress and putting it all together
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep simple, private progress notes and finish your session plan.
This lesson builds toward: After each session, you will write a short, private progress note and celebrate a win, using initials only and never pasting notes into AI.
Short notes help you remember goals and celebrate wins. After each session, write one or two lines: the goal, what you did, one win and the next step. Use first names or initials only, and keep notes where your program says to keep them.
Celebrate progress, even small steps: a raised grade, a finished application, showing up on time. Young people remember when an adult noticed.
Do not paste notes about a young person into AI. If you want help, ask in general terms: "What are fun ways to celebrate a teen raising a grade?"
Step by step:
- After each session, write the goal, what you did, one win and the next step.
- Use initials only and store notes where your program says.
- Celebrate small wins.
- Ask AI only general questions, never about a specific young person.
Words to know:
- Progress note: a short record of what happened and what comes next.
Try it now: Final task: write your 45-minute session plan with AI's help: goal, warm-up, activity, three open questions, an honest AI-use demo for school or careers, and a one-line progress note. Check it against your program's safety rules, then lead it or role-play it with another adult.
You can now plan, lead and track safe mentoring sessions that help young people use AI well.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Session plan Missing the goal, warm-up or activity, or it does not fit 45 minutes. A goal, warm-up, activity, talk and next steps that fit 45 minutes. Changed AI's plan to fit the young person's interests and keep it low-cost. Open questions Fewer than three questions, or yes-or-no questions. Three open questions in the mentor's own words. Includes a plan to repeat back what the mentee says. Honest AI demo The demo has AI doing the work, or skips the school's rules. Shows AI explaining or quizzing, and checking one answer against class materials. Also covers the tool's age rules and the school's AI rules. Progress note No note, or it uses the full name or private details. One line with initials, the goal, a win and the next step. Names where the note will be stored under program rules. Safety and privacy The plan breaks a program safety rule or has private details about the young person. Follows the program's safety rules and has no private details. Lists the reporting steps the mentor would follow if a young person disclosed harm. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How should you name your mentee in progress notes?
check.why: Initials or first name only keep the young person's information private.

check.q: You want ideas to celebrate your mentee's better grade. What do you ask AI?
options: Ask a general question about celebrating a teen's raised grade
check.why: Ask AI only general questions, never about a specific young person.
